stimuli.title: A pinch of iodine
stimuli.content:
For most of us, salt is just salt: something we add to food without a second thought. Yet the packet in an Indian kitchen today usually carries a small word printed on it: 'iodised'. Behind that word lies one of the cheapest and most successful public health measures ever attempted.

The human body needs only a tiny amount of iodine, but it cannot do without it. The thyroid gland in the neck uses iodine to make hormones that control growth and the development of the brain. When the diet lacks iodine, the gland swells, producing a visible lump in the neck known as goitre. The hidden damage is worse. A mother who lacks iodine during pregnancy may give birth to a child whose mental development is permanently held back.

Iodine deficiency is common in hilly regions and in areas prone to floods, where rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil. Crops grown in such soil contain little of it, and so do the people who eat them. For generations, whole villages in the Himalayan foothills were known for the number of people with swollen necks.

The solution that health experts settled on was simple. Instead of asking people to change their diet, they decided to add a little iodine to something everybody already eats every day. Salt was the ideal choice. Rich and poor alike consume it, in roughly similar amounts, and adding iodine to it costs only a few paise per kilogram. India launched a national programme against goitre in the 1960s, and over the following decades iodised salt became the norm in most households.

The work is not finished, however. Some families still buy cheap loose salt from small producers who do not add iodine to it. Iodine can also be lost from salt that is stored carelessly. Damp air, heat and sunlight all cause it to escape, so a packet left open near the stove may slowly lose much of its value.

The advice to households is therefore easy to follow: buy salt that is labelled 'iodised' and keep it in a closed, dry container away from the stove. It is a small habit, but it protects the most valuable thing a child carries into the world: a healthy mind.

stimuli.title: Money nobody claims
stimuli.content:
Somewhere in the records of almost every Indian bank lies money that nobody seems to own. A savings account opened for a scholarship and then forgotten, a fixed deposit made by a grandfather who never told anyone about it, a salary account left behind when its holder moved to another city: such balances add up, across the country, to many thousands of crores of rupees.

Money becomes unclaimed for ordinary reasons. People change jobs and towns and open new accounts without closing the old ones. Small balances seem too trivial to bother about. Most often, an account holder dies and the family simply does not know that the account exists. The passbook may lie in a trunk for years, or there may be no passbook at all.

Banks do not keep this money for themselves. When an account has seen no transaction by its holder for a long time, the bank marks it as inactive and tries to reach the customer. If the deposit remains unclaimed for ten years, the bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India. The money still belongs to the depositor. If the rightful owner or the legal heirs come forward, even many years later, the bank must pay it back.

Claiming it, however, can be a tiring process. Heirs who were never named in the bank's records may have to produce a death certificate, proof of their relationship and sometimes papers from a court, which can take months to obtain.

Much of this trouble can be avoided by one simple step: nomination. When opening an account or making a deposit, a customer can name a person, the nominee, to whom the bank will pay the money after the customer's death. Where a nominee is registered, the bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork. Yet many people leave the nomination form blank, either because they do not understand it or because they find it uncomfortable to think about death.

The Reserve Bank has also set up a website on which people can search for unclaimed deposits held in their own names or in the names of family members. Still, the surest protection lies at home: keep a list of all your accounts, tell your family where the list is kept, and register a nominee for every one of them.

stimuli.title: What seventy per cent means
stimuli.content:
When the weather report says that there is a seventy per cent chance of rain tomorrow, what exactly is it promising? Surveys in several countries have found that people read such forecasts in surprisingly different ways. Some believe that it will rain for seventy per cent of the day. Others think that rain will fall over seventy per cent of the area. A good number simply round the figure up and treat it as a promise of rain.

None of these readings is correct. The figure means that, at any given spot in the forecast area, there is a seven-in-ten chance of at least some measurable rain during the period. Put another way, if the same forecast were issued on a hundred days with similar conditions, rain would be expected on about seventy of them, and on the other thirty it would stay dry.

Where does such a number come from? The atmosphere is so sensitive that a tiny error in today's measurements can grow into a large error in tomorrow's forecast. Forecasters therefore often run their computer models many times, each time starting from slightly different conditions. If most of these runs produce rain at a place, the chance of rain there is high; if only a few do, it is low.

This has an uncomfortable consequence for forecasters. A dry day after a forecast of seventy per cent does not prove that the forecast was wrong; three days in ten are expected to be dry. Yet people tend to remember such days as failures. The fair way to judge a forecaster is over many forecasts: of all the days for which she predicted a seventy per cent chance, did it actually rain on roughly seventy per cent? A forecaster whose figures pass this test is said to be well calibrated, even if she is sometimes 'wrong' on a particular day.

A probability is also more useful than a plain yes or no, because different people can act on it differently. A family planning an outdoor wedding, for whom rain would be a disaster, may hire a tent even when the chance is only thirty per cent. A farmer deciding whether to spray his crop, which a shower would wash off, may wait unless the chance is very low. The same forecast, rightly understood, leads sensible people to different decisions.

stimuli.title: Why the work always takes longer
stimuli.content:
Almost everyone has had the experience. A report that was supposed to take a weekend takes a fortnight; a kitchen that was to be rebuilt in a month is still full of dust after three. Large projects show the same pattern on a grander scale. Flyovers, metro lines and new airports routinely open years after their promised dates and at costs well above their original budgets.

Psychologists have a name for this tendency: the planning fallacy. It describes our habit of underestimating how long our own tasks will take, even when we know that similar tasks in the past took longer than planned. In one well-known study, students were asked to estimate when they would finish their final-year thesis, and also to give a 'worst-case' estimate in case everything went badly. On average, they took longer than even their worst-case estimate.

Why do people who are otherwise sensible keep making the same mistake? Part of the answer lies in how we plan. When we think about a task, we picture the particular steps it requires and imagine them going roughly as intended. This is called taking the 'inside view'. What we leave out are the many things that are not part of the plan at all: an illness, a delayed supplier, a sudden demand from the boss. Each of these is unlikely on its own, but over a long project it is almost certain that some of them will happen.

Memory makes matters worse. When a past project overran, we tend to explain the delay as a special case (the rains came early, a key worker resigned) rather than as a sign of how projects usually go. Having explained the delay away, we expect the next project to run smoothly.

The most effective remedy is to take the 'outside view'. Instead of starting from the details of the plan, a planner first asks how long similar projects actually took, and then adjusts that figure for anything that makes the present case genuinely different. Some governments now require planners of large public works to compare their estimates with the record of comparable projects before a budget is approved.

Curiously, people are often better at predicting how long other people's tasks will take than their own. Asked about a colleague's project, we naturally think of the colleague's past record; asked about our own, we think of our plan. The best forecast for one's own work may come from imagining that it belongs to someone else.

stimuli.title: The pull of the average
stimuli.content:
Many years ago, a psychologist was telling a group of flight instructors that praise teaches better than punishment. One of the instructors objected. In his experience, he said, when he praised a trainee pilot for an unusually smooth landing, the next landing was usually worse; when he shouted at a trainee after a rough one, the next was usually better. Praise, he concluded, made pilots careless, and criticism made them try harder.

His observation was accurate, but his conclusion was not. Any skill performed again and again varies from one attempt to the next. Part of the variation reflects real ability, and part is simply luck: a gust of wind, a moment's distraction. An unusually good landing is likely to have been helped by good luck as well as skill, and luck does not repeat on demand. The next landing will therefore tend to be closer to the trainee's normal standard, that is, worse, whatever the instructor says. In the same way, an unusually bad landing is likely to be followed by a better one. Statisticians call this pattern regression to the mean.

The instructor had been fooled because his words always came at the extremes. He praised only after the best landings and shouted only after the worst, so the natural movement back towards the average looked like the effect of his words.

The same trap appears in many places. Patients tend to visit a doctor when their symptoms are at their worst, and many would improve in the following days even if they did nothing; whatever remedy they took gets the credit. A school that gives extra coaching to the students who did worst in one test will usually find that their next scores rise, even if the coaching is useless. A city that installs speed cameras at the junctions with the most accidents last year will probably see accidents there fall, partly because last year's figures were unusually high.

None of this means that coaching, medicines or speed cameras do not work. It means that a simple before-and-after comparison cannot tell us whether they do. To judge the true effect, we need a comparison group: similar patients who did not take the remedy, or similar junctions, chosen in the same way, where no cameras were installed. Only the difference between the two groups shows what the measure itself achieved.

stimuli.title: A positive result
stimuli.content:
Suppose a disease affects one person in every thousand, and a screening test for it is quite accurate: it correctly detects 99 of every 100 people who have the disease, but it also wrongly flags 5 of every 100 healthy people. A man takes the test and the result is positive. How worried should he be?

Most people, including many doctors when they are asked such questions, guess that he very probably has the disease, perhaps with a chance of 95 per cent. The real answer is surprisingly different. Imagine that 1,00,000 people are tested. About 100 of them have the disease, and the test flags 99 of these. Of the remaining 99,900 healthy people, 5 in every 100, or 4,995, are also flagged. Altogether, 5,094 people test positive, and only 99 of them are actually ill. A positive result therefore means a chance of fewer than 2 in 100 that the man has the disease.

The mistake people make is to ignore how rare the disease is to begin with, a figure statisticians call the base rate. Because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones, even a small error rate among the healthy produces far more false alarms than there are true cases. The test's accuracy, quoted on its own, hides this.

This does not make screening useless. A positive result raises the man's chance of being ill from 1 in 1,000 to nearly 2 in 100, a nearly twenty-fold increase, which is good reason for a second, more precise test. What it does mean is that the first result should be treated as a reason for further checks, not as a diagnosis. It also explains why doctors are often cautious about testing large numbers of people for rare conditions: the anxiety, cost and sometimes risky follow-up procedures suffered by the many healthy people who are wrongly flagged can outweigh the benefit to the few who are truly ill.

The same reasoning applies far beyond medicine. A fraud-detection system at a bank, an airport scanner or any filter that hunts for rare problems among millions of ordinary cases will, unless it is extraordinarily precise, raise far more false alarms than real ones.

stimuli.title: Twenty seconds at the tap
stimuli.content:
Washing hands with soap is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy. Doctors say that the habit can (1) ______ many common illnesses, such as diarrhoea and colds, which spread when germs travel from dirty hands to the mouth, nose or eyes.

Many people believe that rinsing their hands with water is enough. It is not. Germs (2) ______ to the natural oils on our skin, and water alone slides over these oils without removing them. Soap breaks up the oil, so that the germs can be washed away.

How we wash also matters. Hands should be rubbed together with soap for at least twenty seconds, which is about as long as it takes to hum a short song twice. The backs of the hands, the spaces between the fingers and the area under the nails are easily (3) ______, and germs often hide there.

The most important moments to wash are before eating, before cooking or feeding a child, and after using the toilet. Health workers in many villages now teach children to (4) ______ these moments with simple rhymes and with pictures painted on school walls.

Some schools have gone further. They have built long rows of taps near the dining area, so that a whole class can wash at once before the midday meal. Teachers report that children who once (5) ______ the task now rush to the taps, and that fewer pupils stay at home because of stomach infections.

The habit costs very little. A bar of soap is cheap, and where running water is not (6) ______, a simple tap made from a hanging plastic bottle can be enough. It is hard to think of any other medicine that does so much good for so little money.

stimuli.title: One clock for a wide country
stimuli.content:
All of India runs on a single clock. Indian Standard Time, five and a half hours ahead of Greenwich, is based on a line of longitude that (1) ______ near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, roughly in the middle of the country. Whether one lives in Kutch or in Arunachal Pradesh, the clock on the wall shows the same time.

The country, however, is wide. From its western edge to its eastern edge it stretches across nearly thirty degrees of longitude, and the sun rises almost two hours earlier in the far east than in the far west. In the north-east, summer dawn can break before four in the morning, and by the time offices and schools open by the clock, several hours of daylight have already been (2) ______. In the evening, the sun sets early, and homes and offices must switch on their lights, which adds to the demand for electricity.

For this reason, there have long been calls for a second time zone for the north-eastern states. Supporters point out that the tea gardens of Assam have, since colonial days, followed their own local clock, set about an hour ahead of Indian Standard Time, so that work can begin soon after sunrise. They argue that a separate zone would let people make better use of daylight and would (3) ______ electricity.

Opponents are not convinced. They fear that two time zones would cause confusion in railway and airline timetables, where a mistake about the time can have serious (4) ______. Some also argue that a single clock is a symbol of national unity.

Between these positions lies a middle course that has attracted growing attention: keep one time zone, but allow states in the east to (5) ______ their office and school hours, opening and closing earlier than the rest of the country. Such a change would capture much of the benefit of a new zone without redrawing the national clock.

stimuli.title: The tub nobody buys
stimuli.content:
A cinema sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub for ₹150 and a large one for ₹300. Most customers, unwilling to pay double, choose the small tub. Then the cinema adds a third option, a medium tub for ₹280. Hardly anyone buys it, yet sales of the large tub **(1) plummet**.

The medium tub, it turns out, was never meant to be sold. Its job is to make the large tub look like a bargain: for only twenty rupees more than the medium, the customer gets far more popcorn. Marketers call such an option a decoy, and the pattern it creates is known as the decoy effect. The decoy works because people rarely judge prices in **(2) isolation**. Faced with a single price, most of us have little idea whether it is fair. Faced with two options that are easy to compare, we seize on the comparison and let it guide the choice. The decoy is therefore designed to be clearly **(3) superior** to the option the seller wants to sell, yet only slightly cheaper than it, so that the target option wins the comparison.

Subscription offers often use the same trick. A magazine that offers a digital edition for ₹1,000 a year, a print edition for ₹2,500, and print and digital together, also for ₹2,500, is not being generous by **(4) accident**. Few readers want the print edition alone, but its presence makes the combined offer look like a free gift, and the combined offer is what the publisher hoped to sell all along.

Critics argue that decoys **(5) honour** a quirk of the mind rather than serve the customer. Defenders reply that no one is forced to buy anything, and that the decoy merely highlights a deal that genuinely is good value. The truth probably lies between the two. A decoy does not deceive in the way a false label does; every price on the board is real. But it does **(6) steer** choices in a direction the seller has chosen, and a buyer who knows the trick is better placed to ask a simple question: would I still want this option if the decoy were not there?

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what does the thyroid gland use iodine for?

options.text: To protect the neck from damp air and heat
To make hormones that control growth and brain development
To help the stomach digest crops grown in hilly areas
To remove salt that the body does not need

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The thyroid gland in the neck uses iodine to make hormones that control growth and the development of the brain.'
steps: Read what it uses iodine for
Hormones for growth and the brain
solution.why_others_wrong: Removing extra salt, guarding against damp and heat, and digesting crops are never given as the gland's work; damp air and heat are mentioned only as causes of iodine loss from stored salt.
solution.final_answer: Option B: To make hormones that control growth and brain development

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, is iodine deficiency common in hilly and flood-prone areas?

options.text: Rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil.
Salt cannot be carried to these areas during the rains.
The water in these areas destroys iodine in the body.
People in these areas do not like the taste of salt.

solution.concept: Locating a stated cause
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: in such areas 'rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil', so crops, and the people who eat them, get little iodine.
steps: Cause: iodine washed out of the soil
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage never says these people dislike salt, that salt cannot reach them, or that their water destroys iodine in the body.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT given in the passage as a reason why salt was chosen to carry iodine?

options.text: Rich and poor alike consume it.
It keeps its iodine for years even if left open.
Adding iodine to it costs very little.
People eat it in roughly similar amounts.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every reason the passage gives
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 gives three reasons: rich and poor eat salt, in roughly similar amounts, and iodising it costs only a few paise per kilogram. Paragraph 5 says the opposite of the last statement: iodine escapes from salt that is stored carelessly.
steps: Rich and poor consume it: stated
Keeps iodine when left open: contradicted in paragraph 5
solution.why_others_wrong: Eating by rich and poor alike, similar amounts and low cost are all stated in paragraph 4, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It keeps its iodine for years even if left open.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'norm' as used in the passage ('iodised salt became the norm in most households')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: norm = what is usual or standard
solution.explanation: Over the decades iodised salt came to be used in most homes; it became the ordinary, expected thing, i.e. 'the usual practice'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Something found in most households is not 'a rare luxury'. No law is mentioned, so 'a strict rule' goes too far. The passage praises iodised salt, so 'a costly mistake' contradicts it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why does the passage advise keeping salt away from the stove?

options.text: Salt near the stove is easily spilt into food.
Heat causes the iodine in the salt to escape.
Salt near the stove attracts insects.
The stove makes the salt taste bitter.

solution.concept: Inference: linking the advice to the reason given earlier
solution.explanation: Paragraph 5 says that damp air, heat and sunlight cause iodine to escape, so a packet left near the stove loses its value. The advice in the last paragraph follows from this.
steps: Advice: keep salt away from the stove
Earlier reason: heat makes iodine escape
solution.why_others_wrong: Insects, taste and spilling are never mentioned; the only reason the passage gives is the loss of iodine.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Heat causes the iodine in the salt to escape.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: How Salt Is Made from Sea Water
Why Doctors Tell Us to Eat Less Salt
A Small Addition with a Big Benefit

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage explains why the body needs iodine, why salt was chosen to carry it, and how households can keep its benefit. A tiny addition to salt protects health: 'A Small Addition with a Big Benefit'.
steps: Paras 1-3: iodine and the harm its lack causes
solution.why_others_wrong: How salt is made is never described. Himalayan villages appear in one sentence only. The passage is not about eating less salt.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A Small Addition with a Big Benefit

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a reason why money in bank accounts goes unclaimed?

options.text: The family of a dead account holder does not know the account exists.
Some balances are too small to seem worth claiming.
Banks refuse to let customers close their old accounts.
People open new accounts in new towns without closing the old ones.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every reason the passage gives
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives three reasons: people move and open new accounts, small balances seem trivial, and families do not know about a dead relative's account. Nothing is said about banks refusing to close accounts.
steps: Moving without closing old accounts: stated
Family unaware after a death: stated
solution.why_others_wrong: Moving towns, trivial balances and unaware families are all named in paragraph 2, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Banks refuse to let customers close their old accounts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what happens to a deposit that remains unclaimed for ten years?

options.text: The bank adds it to its own profits for that year.
The money is divided among the bank's other customers.
The government spends it on new branches in villages.
The bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'If the deposit remains unclaimed for ten years, the bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.'
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says banks do not keep the money, so it is not added to profits. Spending on new branches and sharing among other customers are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What can be understood from the passage about money that has been moved to the Reserve Bank's fund?

options.text: The owner or the legal heirs can still claim it, even years later.
Only the Reserve Bank can decide whom to give it to.
It can never be returned once it has been moved.
It can be returned only if it is claimed within a month.

solution.concept: Inference from a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says, right after describing the transfer, that 'The money still belongs to the depositor' and that the bank must pay it back if the owner or heirs come forward 'even many years later'.
steps: 'The money still belongs to the depositor'
Can be claimed 'even many years later'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Never returned' and 'only within a month' contradict 'even many years later'. The passage says the bank must pay the rightful owner, not that the Reserve Bank chooses whom to pay.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The owner or the legal heirs can still claim it, even years later.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'trivial' as used in the passage ('Small balances seem too trivial to bother about')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: trivial = of little importance
solution.explanation: People do not bother about small balances because the amounts seem too small to matter, i.e. 'unimportant'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A small balance is not 'dangerous'. 'Valuable' is the opposite of the sense. 'Complicated' does not explain why people would ignore a small sum.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how does registering a nominee help the family?

options.text: The bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork.
The account can never become inactive after a nominee is named.
The bank pays the family a higher rate of interest on the deposit.
The family no longer has to pay any tax on the money.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 5: 'Where a nominee is registered, the bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork.'
steps: Read what happens where one is registered
solution.why_others_wrong: Higher interest, freedom from tax and accounts that never become inactive are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best states the main purpose of the passage?

options.text: To explain why bank deposits go unclaimed and how families can avoid the problem
To criticise banks for hiding unclaimed money from their customers
To describe how the Reserve Bank of India invests the money it receives
To persuade people to keep their savings at home instead of in banks

solution.concept: Main purpose: what the passage as a whole sets out to do
solution.explanation: The passage describes how money becomes unclaimed, what banks do with it, why claiming it is hard, and how nomination, the search website and a list of accounts can prevent the problem. It explains and advises.
steps: Paras 3-4: what happens to it; claims are tiring
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says banks do not keep the money and must pay it back, so it does not accuse them. It never advises keeping savings at home. How the Reserve Bank invests the fund is not discussed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: To explain why bank deposits go unclaimed and how families can avoid the problem

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what does a forecast of 'a seventy per cent chance of rain' actually mean?

options.text: Rain is certain, and it will be heavier than on an ordinary day.
Rain will fall for about seventy per cent of the hours in the day.
Rain will fall over about seventy per cent of the forecast area.
At any spot in the area there is a seven-in-ten chance of some measurable rain.

solution.concept: Locating the stated definition and rejecting the common misreadings
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'at any given spot in the forecast area, there is a seven-in-ten chance of at least some measurable rain during the period.'
steps: Paragraph 2: 'None of these readings is correct'
Correct meaning: seven-in-ten chance at any spot
solution.why_others_wrong: Seventy per cent of the day, seventy per cent of the area and a promise of rain are exactly the misreadings that paragraph 2 rejects.
solution.final_answer: Option D: At any spot in the area there is a seven-in-ten chance of some measurable rain.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, do forecasters run their computer models many times?

options.text: Computers often break down, so each run has to be repeated to get any result at all.
People do not trust a single run, so repeated runs are made to persuade the public.
Each run covers only one town, so many runs are needed to cover a whole country.
Their starting measurements are never perfect, so they test many slightly different starts.

solution.concept: Inference: the reason stated in the same paragraph
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: the atmosphere is so sensitive that 'a tiny error in today's measurements can grow into a large error'. Forecasters 'therefore' run the models many times from slightly different conditions, and the share of runs that give rain sets the chance.
steps: 'Therefore': many runs from slightly different starts
Share of rainy runs → chance of rain
solution.why_others_wrong: Breakdowns, one-town coverage and persuading the public are never mentioned; the passage links repeated runs to the growth of small errors.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Their starting measurements are never perfect, so they test many slightly different starts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Four forecasters each predicted 'a seventy per cent chance of rain' on 40 days. Going by the test described in the passage, whose record shows that he or she is well calibrated?

options.text: The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 40 of the 40 days
The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 12 of the 40 days
The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 28 of the 40 days
The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 20 of the 40 days

solution.concept: Applying the calibration test: the share of rainy days should match the forecast figure
solution.explanation: A well-calibrated forecaster's seventy per cent days should turn out rainy about seventy per cent of the time. Seventy per cent of 40 days = 28 days, so the record '28 of the 40 days' passes the test.
steps: Test: share of rainy days ≈ forecast figure
solution.why_others_wrong: Rain on all 40 days (100%) means the figure was too low, 12 of 40 is 30% and 20 of 40 is 50%; none of these matches seventy per cent. Rain on every day may feel like success, but the passage judges the match between the figure and the outcome.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 28 of the 40 days

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'sensitive' as used in the passage ('The atmosphere is so sensitive that a tiny error ... can grow into a large error')?

options.text: likely to be hurt by criticism

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: one word, several senses; the clause after 'so ... that' fixes the sense
solution.explanation: The atmosphere is called sensitive because a tiny difference in the starting measurements can produce a large difference later. In this sense, 'sensitive' means easily affected by small changes.
steps: 'so sensitive that a tiny error can grow'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hurt by criticism' and 'kept secret' are other senses of 'sensitive' that do not suit the atmosphere. 'Able to detect faint sounds' describes an instrument or an ear, not the weather.
solution.final_answer: Option D: easily affected by small changes

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why might the family planning a wedding and the farmer in the last paragraph act differently on the same forecast?

options.text: Rain would ruin the wedding, while for the farmer it would only waste one spraying.
The farmer wants his crop to be washed by the rain before he sprays it.
The family trusts weather forecasts, while the farmer does not believe them at all.
The family receives a different forecast from the one the farmer receives.

solution.concept: Inference: decisions depend on the cost of being caught by rain, not on the forecast alone
solution.explanation: For the family, rain would be 'a disaster', so even a thirty per cent chance justifies a tent. For the farmer, a shower would only wash off the spray, so he can wait for a day when the chance is very low. The cost of each mistake differs.
steps: Wedding: rain = disaster → act even at 30%
Farmer: rain wastes the spray → spray only when the chance is low
Same forecast, different costs → different decisions
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says both act on 'the same forecast', so a different forecast or distrust is not the reason. The farmer wants to avoid rain washing off the spray, not to have the crop washed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Rain would ruin the wedding, while for the farmer it would only waste one spraying.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Reading the Odds in a Weather Forecast

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through every paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage explains what a percentage chance of rain means, where it comes from, how forecasters should be judged and how people can use it. Its subject is understanding the probability in a forecast.
solution.why_others_wrong: The monsoon is never discussed. The wedding is one example in the last paragraph. Computers are mentioned only as tools for running models, not as replacing weather stations.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Reading the Odds in a Weather Forecast

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What did the study of students' final-year theses described in the passage find?

options.text: Students who gave worst-case estimates always finished on time.
Most students finished well before the dates they had first estimated.
The students' estimates were accurate, but their teachers' were not.
On average, they finished later than their own estimate for things going badly.

solution.concept: Locating a stated finding
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'On average, they took longer than even their worst-case estimate.'
steps: Longer than even the worst case
solution.why_others_wrong: Finishing early, always finishing on time and accurate estimates all contradict the finding; teachers' estimates are not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: On average, they finished later than their own estimate for things going badly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what does taking the 'inside view' of a task involve?

options.text: Imagining one's own planned steps working out more or less as expected
Discussing the plan with colleagues before deciding on a date
Asking how long similar projects carried out by others actually took
Adding a fixed margin of extra time to every estimate one makes

solution.concept: Understanding a term defined in the passage
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'we picture the particular steps it requires and imagine them going roughly as intended. This is called taking the "inside view".'
steps: It is defined by the sentence before it
Picturing one's own steps going to plan
solution.why_others_wrong: Checking how long similar projects took is the 'outside view' of paragraph 5. Adding a margin and consulting colleagues are not what the passage calls the inside view.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Imagining one's own planned steps working out more or less as expected

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, are unplanned events such as an illness or a delayed supplier so damaging to estimates?

options.text: Each of them is very likely to happen on every single day of a project.
Planners include them in their plans, which makes the plans too long.
They happen only on large public projects, which planners cannot control.
Any one of them is improbable, but on a long job a few are bound to occur.

solution.concept: Inference: the reasoning in paragraph 3
solution.explanation: The passage says each such event 'is unlikely on its own, but over a long project it is almost certain that some of them will happen'. Because the inside view leaves them out, the estimate is too short.
steps: Unplanned events are left out of the plan
Each is unlikely, but together they are near-certain
So estimates that ignore them are too short
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage gives everyday examples, so they are not limited to public projects. It calls each event unlikely, not likely every day. The problem is that planners leave such events out, not that they include them.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Any one of them is improbable, but on a long job a few are bound to occur.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'routinely' as used in the passage ('new airports routinely open years after their promised dates')?

options.text: regularly, as a matter of course
deliberately, in order to save money

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: routinely = as a normal, regular occurrence
solution.explanation: The passage says large projects show 'the same pattern', so late openings are the normal state of affairs: they happen regularly, as a matter of course.
steps: Context: 'the same pattern on a grander scale'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rarely' is the opposite of the sense. Nothing suggests the delays are sudden or deliberate; the passage treats them as a common pattern.
solution.final_answer: Option A: regularly, as a matter of course

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of the 'outside view' as the passage describes it?

options.text: A builder ignores his past delays because each had a special cause, such as early rains.
A builder promises an early date because his workers are more skilled than those of his rivals.
A builder lists every step of the new building and adds up the time each step should take.
A builder checks how long the last ten school buildings in the district really took before quoting a date.

solution.concept: Applying a concept: the outside view starts from the record of similar projects
solution.explanation: Paragraph 5: the planner 'first asks how long similar projects actually took'. Checking the actual time taken by ten similar school buildings is exactly this.
steps: Outside view: start from how long similar projects took
Ten past school buildings = similar projects
solution.why_others_wrong: Listing the steps is the inside view. Trusting one's own workers' skill also starts from the details of the present case. Explaining away past delays as special cases is the error described in paragraph 4.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A builder checks how long the last ten school buildings in the district really took before quoting a date.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author suggest in the last paragraph?

options.text: Picturing one's own task as someone else's may give a truer estimate.
Colleagues' tasks always take longer to finish than one's own tasks.
People should ask their colleagues to do their own work for them.
One should never try to estimate how long one's own work will take.

solution.concept: Inference: the conclusion the author draws
solution.explanation: When we judge others' tasks we think of their past record (the outside view), not their plan. So imagining our own task as someone else's may push us to use the record too: 'The best forecast ... may come from imagining that it belongs to someone else.'
steps: Others' tasks → we think of their record
Own task → we think of our plan
So treat one's own task as another's
solution.why_others_wrong: The author suggests imagining, not handing the work to colleagues. Nothing says colleagues' tasks take longer. The author wants better estimates, not no estimates.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Picturing one's own task as someone else's may give a truer estimate.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What did the flight instructor conclude from his experience?

options.text: Praise led to carelessness, while shouting pushed pilots to greater effort.
Praise and criticism had no effect at all on how pilots landed.
Trainee pilots needed more hours of practice before flying alone.
Pilots landed better on calm days than on windy ones.

solution.concept: Locating a stated conclusion
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Praise, he concluded, made pilots careless, and criticism made them try harder.'
solution.why_others_wrong: That praise and criticism had no effect is the psychologist's explanation, not the instructor's belief. Wind and practice hours are not part of his conclusion.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Praise led to carelessness, while shouting pushed pilots to greater effort.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, was the instructor misled?

options.text: His trainees practised in very different weather, so their landings could not be compared.
His praise and criticism came only after extreme landings, so the usual drift back to normal looked like their effect.
He praised the trainees too often, so they stopped paying attention to anything he said.
He remembered the rough landings more clearly than the smooth ones, so he misjudged his trainees.

solution.concept: Inference: identifying the cause of a mistaken conclusion
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'his words always came at the extremes ... so the natural movement back towards the average looked like the effect of his words.' Extreme landings are partly luck, so the next one tends to be more ordinary whatever he says.
steps: Feedback only after the best and worst landings
Next landing drifts back to normal anyway
The drift was mistaken for the effect of the feedback
solution.why_others_wrong: Praising too often contradicts 'praised only after the best landings'. Selective memory and weather differences are not the explanation the passage gives.
solution.final_answer: Option B: His praise and criticism came only after extreme landings, so the usual drift back to normal looked like their effect.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best example of regression to the mean as the passage describes it?

options.text: A batsman scores exactly his average of 40 in every one of his twenty innings.
A batsman who practises harder every season raises his average from 30 to 45 over five years.
A batsman whose average is 40 scores a career-best 180, and then scores 45 in his next innings.
A batsman scores less and less every season as an old knee injury slowly gets worse.

solution.concept: Applying a concept: an extreme result followed by one closer to the usual level
solution.explanation: A career-best 180 is an extreme result, helped by luck as well as skill. The next score, 45, falls back close to his normal average of 40, without any change in ability. That is regression to the mean.
steps: Extreme result: 180 against an average of 40
No change in ability needed → regression to the mean
solution.why_others_wrong: Steady improvement through practice and a steady decline through injury are real changes in ability, not a drift back after an extreme. Scoring exactly 40 every time shows no extreme result at all.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A batsman whose average is 40 scores a career-best 180, and then scores 45 in his next innings.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author imply about the city that installed speed cameras at its most dangerous junctions?

options.text: The city chose the junctions wrongly, because last year's figures were false.
Accidents at those junctions will certainly rise again once the cameras are removed.
A fall in accidents there does not, by itself, show how much the cameras helped.
The cameras were useless and the money should have been spent elsewhere.

solution.concept: Inference: the author's qualified position
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says accidents will 'probably' fall 'partly because last year's figures were unusually high'. Paragraph 5 adds that this does not mean cameras do not work, only that a before-and-after comparison cannot tell us; comparable junctions without cameras are needed.
steps: Junctions chosen at an extreme year
Need a comparison group to measure the real effect
solution.why_others_wrong: The author says plainly that this does not mean cameras do not work. Nothing predicts what happens when cameras are removed. Last year's figures were unusually high, not false.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A fall in accidents there does not, by itself, show how much the cameras helped.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: As used in the passage ('luck does not repeat on demand'), the phrase 'on demand' means

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: on demand = as soon as or whenever it is asked for
solution.explanation: Good luck helped the smooth landing, but the trainee cannot call it up again whenever he wants it; luck does not come back 'on demand'.
steps: It cannot be produced again at will
solution.why_others_wrong: 'At a high price' and 'under a legal order' are senses linked to demand in trade and law, not here. 'After a long delay' says nothing about luck being available at will.
solution.final_answer: Option B: whenever it is wanted

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?

solution.concept: Tone: how the author treats the subject
solution.explanation: The author explains a statistical pattern with examples and warns readers not to trust simple before-and-after comparisons. That is explanatory and cautionary.
steps: Explains: luck, extremes, regression to the mean
solution.why_others_wrong: The author does not attack the instructor or anyone else, so the tone is not angry. The subject is treated seriously, not as a joke, and there is no longing for the past.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why do most of the positive results in the example come from healthy people?

options.text: Healthy people so outnumber sick ones that a small error rate among them yields many false alarms.
The disease often disappears on its own between the test and the result.
Most people who take the test have already been told by a doctor that they are ill.
The test is much better at detecting the disease in healthy people than in sick ones.

solution.concept: Inference: the base-rate reasoning in paragraph 3
solution.explanation: There are 99,900 healthy people and only 100 sick ones. Flagging just 5 in 100 healthy people gives 4,995 false alarms, far more than the 99 true cases. Paragraph 3 states this reason.
steps: 5% of 99,900 = 4,995 false alarms vs 99 true cases
Rarity of the disease → most positives are false
solution.why_others_wrong: The test detects 99 of every 100 sick people; it does not 'detect the disease' in healthy people better. Prior diagnosis and recovery between test and result are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Healthy people so outnumber sick ones that a small error rate among them yields many false alarms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Suppose the same test (detecting 99 of every 100 sick people and wrongly flagging 5 of every 100 healthy people) were used for a disease that affects 1 person in every 100. Using the method of the passage, roughly what share of the people who test positive would actually be ill?

solution.concept: Applying the passage's method (count people, not percentages) to a new base rate
solution.explanation: Out of 1,00,000 people, 1,000 are ill and the test flags 990 of them. Of the 99,000 healthy people, 5 in 100 = 4,950 are flagged. Positives = 990 + 4,950 = 5,940, of whom 990 are ill: 990/5,940 = 1/6.
solution.shortcut: Positives ≈ 990 true + 4,950 false; 990 is one sixth of 5,940
solution.why_others_wrong: 'About 99 in 100' and 'about 95 in 100' confuse the test's accuracy with the chance that a positive person is ill, the very error the passage warns against. 'About 1 in 50' is the passage's own answer for the rarer disease, before the base rate was changed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the author, how should a first positive result from such a screening test be treated?

options.text: As a sign that the screening test should be stopped for everyone
As a meaningless result, since the test cannot be trusted at all
As a reason for a second, more precise test rather than as a diagnosis
As proof that the person certainly has the disease and needs treatment

solution.concept: Inference: the author's conclusion in paragraph 4
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'the first result should be treated as a reason for further checks, not as a diagnosis', since it raises the chance of illness nearly twenty-fold and justifies 'a second, more precise test'.
steps: Positive result raises the chance nearly twenty-fold
But the chance is still under 2 in 100
solution.why_others_wrong: Treating the result as proof is the mistake the passage corrects. Calling it meaningless or stopping screening contradicts 'This does not make screening useless'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: As a reason for a second, more precise test rather than as a diagnosis

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'outweigh' as used in the passage ('can outweigh the benefit to the few who are truly ill')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: outweigh = be greater or more important than
solution.explanation: The author explains why doctors are cautious: the harm done to many wrongly flagged healthy people can be greater than the good done to the few sick ones. To 'outweigh' is to be greater than.
steps: Two things compared: harm to many vs benefit to few
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Be equal to' would give doctors no reason for caution. 'Be hidden by' and 'be paid for by' do not express a comparison of size.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the effect of a healthy habit on illness
solution.explanation: The passage praises handwashing as a way 'to stay healthy'. A healthy habit stops illnesses from happening: it can 'prevent' them.
steps: 'one of the simplest ways to stay healthy'
solution.why_others_wrong: A habit that keeps people healthy does not 'cause' illness. Illnesses are not 'enjoyed', and 'measure' says nothing about keeping them away.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: why water alone does not remove germs
solution.explanation: Water slides over the oils 'without removing them', so the germs stay held by the oils. Germs 'stick to' the oils on the skin.
steps: Because germs are held by the skin's oils
solution.why_others_wrong: Germs do not 'speak' or 'point' to oils. 'Travel to the oils' does not explain why water fails to remove them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the parts of the hand that are overlooked
solution.explanation: The backs of the hands, the spaces between the fingers and the area under the nails are places people forget to wash, which is why 'germs often hide there'. They are easily 'missed'.
steps: These places are not washed properly
solution.why_others_wrong: Hands are not 'painted', 'praised' or 'borrowed' while washing; none of these explains why germs hide there.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the purpose of rhymes and pictures
solution.explanation: Rhymes and pictures on school walls are memory aids. They help children 'remember' the moments when they must wash their hands.
steps: Purpose: keep the moments in mind
solution.why_others_wrong: Health workers would not teach children to 'forget' or 'hide' the moments. 'Count' the moments does not suit rhymes meant to build a habit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'once ... now' signals a change of behaviour
solution.explanation: 'Children who once ___ the task now rush to the taps' contrasts their past and present attitudes. Children who now rush to wash once kept away from it: they 'avoided' the task.
solution.why_others_wrong: If they had 'enjoyed' the task, there would be no change to report. Children did not 'invent' or 'order' handwashing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: when a substitute tap is needed
solution.explanation: A tap made from a hanging bottle is a substitute used where there is no running water: where it is not 'available'.
steps: Needed where running water cannot be had
solution.why_others_wrong: Whether water is 'heavy', 'noisy' or 'silent' has nothing to do with needing a bottle tap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: how a line of longitude relates to a place
solution.explanation: A line of longitude runs from pole to pole, so it does not begin or stop at a town; it 'passes' near it. IST is based on the line that passes near Mirzapur.
steps: Line of longitude: runs north-south across the whole globe
It crosses places, it does not end in them
solution.why_others_wrong: A line of longitude neither 'begins' nor 'stops' near a town, and lines do not 'settle'. Only 'passes' describes a line running past a place.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the cost of opening late by the sun's clock
solution.explanation: Dawn breaks before four, but offices open hours later by the clock, so those early hours of daylight go unused. They have been 'wasted', which is the problem the paragraph describes.
solution.why_others_wrong: Daylight that passes before work starts is not 'saved', 'earned' or 'stored'; each of these turns the problem into a benefit, while the paragraph is listing costs.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the benefit claimed by supporters
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 said early sunsets add to the demand for electricity. Supporters argue that a separate zone would make better use of daylight and so reduce that demand: it would 'save' electricity.
steps: Problem: early sunset → more electricity for lights
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Consume' and 'waste' would make the supporters argue against their own proposal. 'Measure' electricity is not a benefit of a time zone.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what follows from a mistake in a timetable
solution.explanation: Opponents fear confusion in railway and airline timetables, where a mistake about the time can lead to serious results such as missed connections or accidents. Results of an action are its 'consequences'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A mistake does not have serious 'rewards'. 'Intentions' and 'origins' come before an action, not after it, so they cannot express the danger the opponents fear.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the phrase after the blank explains it
solution.explanation: The words that follow, 'opening and closing earlier than the rest of the country', show that the hours would be moved earlier. To move a time earlier is to 'advance' it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Postpone' would move the hours later, the opposite of 'earlier'. Offices cannot 'abolish' or 'conceal' their hours and still open earlier.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'Hardly anyone buys it, yet sales of the large tub plummet'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the rest of the passage shows what the decoy does to the target option
solution.explanation: The passage explains that the medium tub exists 'to make the large tub look like a bargain'. Its effect is that more people buy the large tub, so its sales rise sharply: they 'soar'. 'Plummet' (fall steeply) says the opposite.
steps: Purpose of the medium tub: make the large tub look like a bargain
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Stagnate' and 'vanish' would mean the decoy failed, yet the passage presents it as a working trick. 'Plummet' contradicts the purpose of the decoy, so it cannot stay.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'The decoy works because people rarely judge prices in isolation'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the next two sentences explain the bold word
solution.explanation: The passage goes on to say that with a single price we cannot tell whether it is fair, but with two options we 'seize on the comparison'. So people rarely judge a price on its own, 'in isolation'. The word is correct.
steps: Single price: we cannot judge it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In comparison' reverses the point: the passage says people almost always compare. 'Haste' and 'silence' have nothing to do with how prices are judged.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'The decoy is therefore designed to be clearly superior to the option the seller wants to sell, yet only slightly cheaper than it'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: checking the bold word against the example
solution.explanation: The medium tub (₹280) gives far less popcorn than the large one (₹300) for only twenty rupees less: it is clearly worse value, i.e. 'inferior' to the target option. A decoy that was 'superior' would win the comparison itself.
steps: Example: medium = much less popcorn, only ₹20 cheaper
So it is clearly worse than the large tub
solution.why_others_wrong: An 'identical' option could not be both identical and cheaper, and an 'unrelated' option could not be compared at all. 'Superior' contradicts the example, so a replacement is needed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'is not being generous by accident'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'not ... by accident' = deliberately
solution.explanation: The next sentence explains that the print-only option is there so that the combined offer looks like a free gift, which is 'what the publisher hoped to sell all along'. The apparent generosity is deliberate, i.e. not 'by accident'. The word is correct.
steps: Following sentence: the publisher planned it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Not generous by force' or 'by law' suggests the publisher was compelled, and 'by habit' suggests routine; the passage is about a deliberate design.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'Critics argue that decoys honour a quirk of the mind rather than serve the customer'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: what critics would say a decoy does to a weakness
solution.explanation: Critics object that decoys take unfair advantage of a quirk in how people judge prices, instead of serving the customer. To take unfair advantage of something is to 'exploit' it. 'Honour' (respect) is not a criticism.
steps: Charge: taking advantage of a mental quirk
solution.why_others_wrong: Critics would not say decoys 'conceal' or 'cure' the quirk; decoys depend on it. 'Honour' turns the criticism into praise, so it must be replaced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (6) may be wrongly used: 'But it does steer choices in a direction the seller has chosen'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: a decoy guides choices without forcing them
solution.explanation: A decoy pushes buyers towards the option the seller prefers, while leaving them free to choose. To guide something in a chosen direction is to 'steer' it. The word is correct.
steps: Decoy: guides buyers to the target option
'in a direction the seller has chosen'
solution.why_others_wrong: A decoy does not 'halt' or 'ignore' choices, and 'record choices in a direction' makes no sense. Only 'steer' goes with 'in a direction'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
My younger sister is (A) / more cleverer than (B) / all her classmates. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Double comparative: a comparative adjective is formed either with -er or with 'more', never both
solution.explanation: 'Cleverer' is already comparative, so adding 'more' doubles the comparison. Correct: 'My younger sister is cleverer than all her classmates.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject and verb. Part C ('than all her classmates') correctly completes the comparison. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The teacher said us (A) / to keep our bags (B) / outside the laboratory. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Say' does not take a person as its direct object; 'tell' does (tell someone to do something)
solution.explanation: We 'tell' someone to do something, or 'say' something 'to' someone. Correct: 'The teacher told us to keep our bags outside the laboratory.'
steps: 'said us' → 'told us': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('to keep our bags') correctly gives the instruction, and part C is a correct place phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The teacher said us

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The shepherd counted (A) / his sheep carefully (B) / before closing the gate. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Error-free sentence: 'sheep' has the same form in the singular and the plural
solution.explanation: 'Sheep' does not add -s in the plural, so 'his sheep' is correct for a whole flock. 'Counted ... carefully' and 'before closing the gate' are also correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B only looks wrong to a reader who expects 'sheeps'; parts A and C have no error either, so 'No error' is the answer.

questions.question_text:

Every evening, the old man sat (A) / by the window and (B) / heard to the news on the radio. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Every evening, the old man sat
heard to the news on the radio.

solution.concept: Hear vs listen: 'listen to' means to pay attention to a sound; 'hear' takes no 'to'
solution.explanation: Paying attention to the news every evening is 'listening to' it. 'Heard to' is wrong. Correct: '... and listened to the news on the radio.'
steps: Deliberate attention to a sound → listen to
'heard to' → 'listened to': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A (time phrase, subject and verb) and part B ('by the window and') are correct. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

Our school team won the visitors (A) / by three goals to one (B) / in the final match. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Our school team won the visitors

solution.concept: Win vs beat: one wins a match, a game or a prize; one beats an opponent
solution.explanation: The visitors are the opponents, so the verb must be 'beat': 'Our school team beat the visitors by three goals to one ...'. One could say 'won the match', but not 'won the visitors'.
steps: Object of the verb: the visitors (opponents)
'won the visitors' → 'beat the visitors': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('by three goals to one') and part C ('in the final match') are correct. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

This small car is very economic (A) / because it uses (B) / very little petrol. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: This small car is very economic

solution.concept: Economic (relating to the economy) vs economical (giving good value, not wasteful)
solution.explanation: A car that uses very little petrol saves money: it is 'economical'. 'Economic' means 'relating to the economy', as in 'economic growth'.
steps: Meaning needed: cheap to run, not wasteful
'very economic' → 'very economical': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('because it uses') and part C ('very little petrol') are correct. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

Hearing the doorbell, (A) / she quickly wore her coat (B) / and ran down the stairs. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Wear (be dressed in: a state) vs put on (the action of dressing)
solution.explanation: Grabbing a coat and getting into it is an action done 'quickly': she 'put on' her coat. 'Wear' describes having clothes on, not the act of dressing.
steps: 'wore her coat' → 'put on her coat': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct participle phrase with 'she' as its subject. Part C is correct. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
We had expected the repairs to be cheap, (A) / but in the end they (B) / costed us twelve thousand rupees. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: We had expected the repairs to be cheap,

solution.concept: 'Cost' (to have a price) has the same form in the past tense: cost, cost, cost
solution.explanation: The past tense of 'cost' in the sense of having a price is 'cost': 'they cost us twelve thousand rupees'. ('Costed' is used only for working out a cost, as in 'The plan was costed by the engineers'.)
steps: 'costed us' → 'cost us': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A ('had expected ... to be cheap') and part B ('but in the end they') are correct. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: costed us twelve thousand rupees.

Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
After a six-hour journey (A) / over mountain roads, the bus (B) / finally arrived to the village. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Arrive' takes 'at' (a point or building) or 'in' (a town, village or country), never 'to'
solution.explanation: One arrives 'in' a town or village and 'at' a station or building. 'Arrived to' is wrong: '... the bus finally arrived in the village.'
steps: arrive in (village, town) / arrive at (station, building)
'arrived to' → 'arrived in': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A and part B ('over mountain roads, the bus') are correct. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: finally arrived to the village.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
On reaching the hospital, (A) / we learnt that the doctor (B) / had already left for the day. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: had already left for the day.

solution.concept: Error-free sentence: a participle phrase must refer to the subject of the main clause; past perfect for the earlier action
solution.explanation: 'On reaching the hospital' refers to 'we', the subject of the main clause, so the phrase is correctly attached. The doctor's leaving happened before 'we learnt', so 'had already left' is correct.
steps: Who reached? 'we' = subject of the main clause: correct
Earlier past action: 'had already left': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The opening phrase is not dangling, since its subject is 'we'. 'Learnt' and 'had already left' are in the right order of time. No part has an error.

After the conference, (A) / the delegates returned (B) / to their respectable hotels. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Respective (belonging to each one separately) vs respectable (deserving respect; decent)
solution.explanation: Each delegate went back to his or her own hotel: 'their respective hotels'. 'Respectable hotels' would comment on the hotels' reputation, which is not the sense.
steps: Sense: each to his or her own hotel
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A (time phrase) and part B ('the delegates returned') are correct. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: to their respectable hotels.

The old poet's childish delight (A) / in birdsong and falling rain (B) / charmed everyone who met him. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Childish (silly, immature: a criticism) vs childlike (having a child's innocence and freshness: praise)
solution.explanation: The delight 'charmed everyone', so the author is praising the poet's innocent sense of wonder. That is 'childlike delight'. 'Childish' is used to criticise immature behaviour.
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('in birdsong and falling rain') correctly follows 'delight', and part C is correct. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The old poet's childish delight
