questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
His efforts notwithstanding, (A) / the project could not be (B) / completed on time. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Error-free sentence: 'notwithstanding' (= in spite of) may stand after its noun
solution.explanation: 'Notwithstanding' can come before or after the noun it governs: 'notwithstanding his efforts' or 'his efforts notwithstanding'. 'Could not be completed' is a correct passive. The sentence means that the project was late in spite of his efforts.
steps: 'His efforts notwithstanding' = in spite of his efforts: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The position of 'notwithstanding' may look odd, but it is correct. Parts B and C form a correct passive. No part has an error.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Although she has lived in Paris for only a year, she speaks French **very fluent**.

solution.concept: An adverb, not an adjective, describes how an action is done
solution.explanation: 'Fluent' is an adjective; it describes the action 'speaks', so the adverb 'fluently' is needed: 'she speaks French very fluently'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Very fluency' puts a noun where a modifier is needed. 'Much fluent' keeps the adjective. The original uses an adjective for a verb, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The lecture went on for three hours, and most of the students **felt boring**.

solution.concept: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels; -ing adjectives describe what causes the feeling
solution.explanation: The students had the feeling, so they 'felt bored'. The lecture was 'boring' because it caused that feeling.
steps: Who has the feeling? The students
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Felt boringly' uses an adverb after a linking verb. 'Were feeling boring' still says the students caused boredom. 'Felt boring' is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Your handwriting is very **similar with** your brother's.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: similar to
solution.explanation: The adjective 'similar' is followed by 'to': 'Your handwriting is very similar to your brother's.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Similar from' confuses it with 'different from', and 'similar than' with comparatives. 'Similar with' is not standard, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
I don't eat meat, and my sister **does not eat it too**.

solution.concept: 'Too' and 'also' are used in positive statements; 'either' adds a negative statement to another
solution.explanation: The added statement is negative ('does not eat it'), so it ends with 'either': 'my sister does not eat it either'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Also' has the same problem as 'too'. 'Does not ... neither' is a double negative. The original uses 'too' with a negative, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: does not eat it either

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
After retiring from the army, he **went on becoming** one of the most successful farmers in the district.

solution.concept: 'Go on to do' = do something next, after something else; 'go on doing' = continue doing the same thing
solution.explanation: Becoming a farmer was the next stage of his life after the army, not something he kept doing before. So the pattern is 'went on to become'.
steps: Sense: a new stage after retiring
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Went on to becoming' mixes the two patterns, and 'went on become' drops 'to'. 'Went on becoming' would mean he continued becoming a farmer, which makes no sense, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: went on to become

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Many economists believe that a gradual reform **is more preferable to** a sudden one.

solution.concept: 'Preferable' already means 'better' or 'more desirable', so it does not take 'more'; it is followed by 'to'
solution.explanation: 'Preferable' contains the idea of comparison, so 'more preferable' is redundant. The pattern is 'preferable to': 'a gradual reform is preferable to a sudden one'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'More preferable than' keeps the redundant 'more' and adds the wrong preposition. 'Preferable than' uses the wrong preposition. The original is redundant, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
We **regret informing** you that your application for the post of librarian has not been accepted.

solution.concept: 'Regret to do' = be sorry about what one is about to say or do (formal announcements); 'regret doing' = be sorry for something already done
solution.explanation: The writer is sorry about the news being given now, in this letter. That sense takes the to-infinitive: 'We regret to inform you ...'. 'Regret informing' would mean being sorry for having informed someone earlier.
steps: Sense: sorry about what we are now telling you
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Regret to informing' mixes the two patterns. 'Are regretting to inform' puts a verb of feeling in the continuous form. 'Regret informing' gives the wrong meaning, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Try as he might**, the old man could not loosen the rusty bolt.

solution.concept: Concessive inversion: verb (base form) + as + subject + might = however hard he tried
solution.explanation: 'Try as he might' is a fixed concessive pattern meaning 'however hard he tried'. It is correct as it stands.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Trying as he might' breaks the fixed pattern, 'Try as might he' inverts the wrong words, and 'As he might try' loses the concessive meaning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Accepting the job in Delhi would **mean to leave** my parents alone in the village.

solution.concept: 'Mean doing' = involve or result in; 'mean to do' = intend to do
solution.explanation: The sentence says what accepting the job would involve: leaving the parents alone. For this sense 'mean' takes the -ing form: 'would mean leaving my parents alone'.
steps: Subject: accepting the job (a thing, not a person)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Mean to leave' would mean 'intend to leave', which a job cannot do. 'Mean to leaving' mixes the patterns. 'Meant to leave' clashes with 'would', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Before leaving for the city, he gave his younger brother **the few rupees** he had saved.

solution.concept: 'The few' + plural countable noun = all of a small number (here, all the rupees he had saved)
solution.explanation: 'Rupees' is countable, so 'few' is right, and 'the few rupees he had saved' means all of the small number of rupees he had. The phrase is correct.
steps: 'the few ... he had saved' = all of a small number
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Little' goes with uncountable nouns, so 'the little rupees' and 'a little rupees' are wrong. 'Few of rupees' needs 'the' before the noun.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The plane **took up** an hour late because of the fog.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: take off = (of an aircraft) leave the ground
solution.explanation: A plane leaving the ground 'takes off': 'The plane took off an hour late because of the fog.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Took over' means took control, and 'took in' means received or deceived. 'Took up' (started a hobby or used space) is wrong here, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Thieves **broke from** the shop last night and stole two laptops.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: break into (a building) = enter it by force
solution.explanation: The thieves forced their way into the shop to steal the laptops: they 'broke into' it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Broke up' means ended or separated, and 'broke down' means stopped working. 'Broke from' is not the phrase for a forced entry, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
While shopping in the market, I **ran across** my old school teacher.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: run across (someone) = meet by chance
solution.explanation: Meeting a teacher unexpectedly while shopping is 'running across' him or her. The phrase is correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Ran over' means hit with a vehicle, 'ran through' means rehearsed or pierced, and 'ran off' means escaped; none describes a chance meeting.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The witness's story did not **add on**; the times he gave did not match the bus timetable.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: add up (informal) = make sense; be consistent
solution.explanation: The witness's times clashed with the timetable, so his story did not make sense: it did not 'add up'.
steps: Clue: times did not match the timetable
Story not consistent → did not add up
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Add in' means include, and 'add to' needs an object (add to something). 'Add on' means attach an extra part, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The opposition tried hard to **pick holes on** the government's new housing plan.

solution.concept: Idiom: pick holes in (something) = find faults in it
solution.explanation: Looking for faults in a plan is 'picking holes in' it: 'The opposition tried hard to pick holes in the government's new housing plan.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'At' and 'from' are not used in this phrase, and neither is 'on', so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The company tried to **hush away** the scandal, but a junior employee leaked the documents to the press.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: hush up = keep something secret, especially something discreditable
solution.explanation: The company wanted to stop the scandal from becoming known; the leak defeated that aim. Keeping a scandal secret is 'hushing it up'.
steps: Clue: the documents were leaked despite the company
Keeping a scandal quiet → hush up
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hush down' and 'hush off' are not English phrasal verbs, and neither is 'hush away', so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The dam was completed **in the teeth of** fierce opposition from the villages that it would flood.

solution.concept: Idiom: in the teeth of = in spite of (strong opposition or difficulty)
solution.explanation: The dam was built despite fierce opposition. 'In the teeth of' means exactly this, so the phrase is correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In the jaws of' means close to (danger or death), as in 'in the jaws of death'. 'On the teeth of' and 'at the teeth of' are not idioms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: There are too much cars on this narrow road.
There are too many cars on this narrow road.
There is too many cars on this narrow road.
There are too more cars on this narrow road.

solution.concept: 'Many' with countable plural nouns; 'much' with uncountable nouns; verb agrees with the plural noun
solution.explanation: 'Cars' is a countable plural, so it takes 'many' and the plural verb 'are': 'There are too many cars on this narrow road.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Too much cars' uses 'much' with a countable noun, 'too more' is not English, and 'There is ... cars' does not agree with the plural noun.
solution.final_answer: Option B: There are too many cars on this narrow road.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: Only a small amount of sugar is needed for this recipe.
A large number of people gathered outside the stadium.
A large amount of money was spent on the new stadium.
A large amount of people gathered outside the stadium.

solution.concept: 'Amount of' goes with uncountable nouns; 'number of' with countable plurals
solution.explanation: 'People' is countable, so it takes 'a large number of'. 'A large amount of people' is incorrect.
steps: Only the people-with-'amount' sentence is wrong
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Amount of money' and 'amount of sugar' correctly pair 'amount' with uncountable nouns, and 'number of people' correctly pairs 'number' with a countable plural.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A large amount of people gathered outside the stadium.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: I want that you come early tomorrow.
I want you come early tomorrow.
I want you to come early tomorrow.
I want that you should come early tomorrow.

solution.concept: 'Want' takes object + to-infinitive, not a that-clause
solution.explanation: The pattern is 'want + someone + to do something': 'I want you to come early tomorrow.'
steps: 'I want you to come early tomorrow.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Want' is not followed by a that-clause, with or without 'should'. 'Want you come' leaves out the 'to' of the infinitive.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I want you to come early tomorrow.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: Each passenger on the night bus was given a blanket.
Nearly every seat on the night bus was taken.
Almost every passenger on the night bus was asleep.
Almost each passenger on the night bus was asleep.

solution.concept: 'Almost' and 'nearly' combine with 'every', not with 'each'
solution.explanation: 'Each' picks out members one by one and cannot be modified by 'almost'; 'every' sees the group as a whole and can. So 'Almost each passenger ...' is incorrect; it should be 'Almost every passenger ...'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Almost every passenger' and 'Nearly every seat' use 'every' correctly, and 'Each passenger was given a blanket' uses 'each' without 'almost', which is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Almost each passenger on the night bus was asleep.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) So the puppy stayed, and the children named him Bholu and took turns to share their lunch with him.
(B) One rainy morning, a thin, shivering puppy was found sitting at the gate of our village school.
(C) The headmistress at first wanted to send him away, as she was worried that he might bite.
(D) Today Bholu sleeps outside the staffroom and barks loudly whenever a stranger comes near the school.
(E) But when she saw how gently he played with the youngest pupils, she changed her mind.

solution.concept: Para jumble: arrival → first reaction → change of mind → result ('So') → present day
solution.explanation: B introduces the puppy. C gives the headmistress's first reaction. E ('But when she saw ...') reverses it. A ('So the puppy stayed') is the result of her change of mind. D ('Today') ends the story.
steps: B → C: her first reaction ('at first')
C → E: 'But ... she changed her mind'
E → A ('So the puppy stayed') → D ('Today'): BCEAD
solution.why_others_wrong: BACED says 'So the puppy stayed' before any question of sending him away has arisen. BCAED puts A between the headmistress's doubt and her change of mind, so 'So' has no reason before it. CBEAD opens with 'him', who has not yet been introduced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Making a cup of masala tea is easier than many people think.
(P) Then add the tea leaves and let them boil for a minute, until the water turns dark.
(Q) Finally, strain the tea into cups and serve it hot.
(R) First, bring a cup of water to the boil with some crushed ginger and a few cardamoms.
(S) After that, pour in the milk and sugar and let the mixture come to the boil once more.

solution.concept: Process jumble: sequence words (First, Then, After that, Finally) and the logic of the steps
solution.explanation: R ('First') starts with boiling water and spices. P ('Then') adds tea leaves to the water. S ('After that') adds milk and sugar. Q ('Finally') strains and serves.
steps: R → P: 'Then' add tea leaves to the water
P → S: 'After that' milk and sugar
S → Q: 'Finally' strain and serve: RPSQ
solution.why_others_wrong: RSPQ adds milk before the tea leaves, yet P speaks of 'the water' turning dark. PRSQ starts with 'Then'. RPQS serves the tea before the milk and sugar are added.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) At sea level, water boils at 100 °C, and no amount of extra heat can make it hotter while it stays liquid in an open pan.
(B) Food that would take an hour to cook in an open pot can therefore be ready in a fraction of that time.
(C) A pressure cooker gets round this limit by sealing the pot so that the steam cannot escape.
(D) The trapped steam raises the pressure inside, and at this higher pressure water boils only at around 120 °C.
(E) Cooks in hill towns value the device even more, because at high altitude water boils below 100 °C and food in an open pan cooks very slowly.

solution.concept: Para jumble: the limit → how the cooker gets round it → the mechanism → the result → a further use
solution.explanation: A states the limit of an open pan. C ('this limit') shows how the cooker gets round it. D explains how sealing raises the boiling point. B ('therefore') gives the result: faster cooking. E adds why hill cooks value it even more.
steps: C → D: trapped steam → higher pressure → hotter water
D → B ('therefore' faster) → E ('even more'): ACDBE
solution.why_others_wrong: ACBDE gives the result ('therefore') before the higher temperature that causes it. CDABE opens with 'this limit', which has nothing to refer to. ACDEB places 'therefore' after E, so it would wrongly follow from the hill-town point instead of from D.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) During a storm, we always see the flash of lightning before we hear the thunder, although both are produced at the same moment.
(P) Light travels so fast that the flash reaches us almost instantly.
(Q) Sound, by contrast, covers only about a third of a kilometre every second.
(R) The reason is the great difference between the speeds of light and sound.
(S) By counting the seconds between the flash and the bang and dividing by three, one can therefore estimate roughly how many kilometres away the storm is.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'The reason' → light → 'by contrast' sound → 'therefore' practical use
solution.explanation: R ('The reason') explains the puzzle in (1). P describes light, and Q ('by contrast') describes sound. S ('therefore') uses the third-of-a-kilometre figure from Q to estimate distance.
steps: Q → S: 'dividing by three' uses Q's figure: RPQS
solution.why_others_wrong: RQPS puts 'by contrast' before the thing it contrasts with. PQRS gives the details before 'The reason' introduces them. RPSQ divides by three before the speed of sound (a third of a kilometre a second) is given.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) that he fell asleep
(Q) the night watchman was
(R) in his chair within minutes.
(S) so tired

solution.concept: 'So + adjective + that' (result clause)
solution.explanation: 'The night watchman was so tired that he fell asleep in his chair within minutes.' Subject and verb (Q), 'so tired' (S), the result clause (P) and the place and time phrase that ends the sentence (R).
steps: that-clause: P, completed by R (ends with the full stop)
solution.why_others_wrong: QPSR separates 'so tired' from 'was'. SQPR opens with 'so tired', which has no verb before it. QSRP puts 'in his chair within minutes.' (which ends with the full stop) before the result clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) much as
(Q) I cannot support
(R) I admire my uncle's courage,
(S) his plan to sell the land.

solution.concept: Concessive 'much as' (= although ... very much) + main clause
solution.explanation: 'Much as I admire my uncle's courage, I cannot support his plan to sell the land.' The concessive clause (P + R) comes first, then the main clause (Q + S), which ends with the full stop.
steps: Concessive clause: much as (P) + I admire my uncle's courage, (R)
Main clause: I cannot support (Q) + his plan to sell the land. (S)
solution.why_others_wrong: RPQS puts 'much as' after the clause it belongs to. PQRS gives 'Much as I cannot support', which reverses the logic and leaves 'I admire ...' hanging. QPSR splits 'I cannot support' from its object.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The medicine tasted so ______ that the little boy spat it out.

solution.concept: Single blank: the result clause ('so ... that he spat it out') decides the word
solution.explanation: A child spits out medicine that tastes unpleasant. 'Bitter' gives that unpleasant taste.
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'sweet', 'fresh' or 'mild' taste would not make the boy spit the medicine out.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The shopkeeper ______ the boy for the broken glass and asked him to ______ for it.

solution.concept: Double blank: both words must fit the situation of a broken glass
solution.explanation: The shopkeeper holds the boy responsible for breaking the glass ('blamed') and wants the cost covered ('pay for it').
steps: Broken glass → the boy is held responsible: blamed
'asked him to ___ for it' → pay for it
solution.why_others_wrong: No one is 'praised' or 'thanked' for breaking a glass. 'Wait for it' does not suit a shopkeeper's demand after damage.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Unlike her evasive colleagues, the witness was ______: she answered every question directly and hid nothing.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'Unlike' signals a contrast, and the colon gives the definition
solution.explanation: She answered directly and hid nothing, the opposite of her evasive colleagues. Someone who speaks plainly and openly is 'forthright'.
steps: 'Unlike her evasive colleagues' → the opposite of evasive
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Devious' and 'cunning' describe someone who hides the truth, like the colleagues. 'Hesitant' does not fit someone who answered every question directly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The new parking fee was deeply ______ by small traders, who held protests in every market.

solution.concept: Single blank: the traders' reaction ('held protests') decides the word
solution.explanation: People who protest in every market feel bitter about the fee. To feel bitter at something unfair is to 'resent' it: the fee was deeply 'resented'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Traders who 'welcomed' or 'admired' the fee would not protest, and a fee that was 'ignored' would not cause protests in every market.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The ______ child refused to share his toys and ______ for hours whenever he did not get his way.

solution.concept: Double blank: both words must describe a child who refuses to share
solution.explanation: A child who will not share and is unhappy whenever he does not get his way is 'spoilt', and he 'sulked' (was silently bad-tempered) for hours.
steps: Refuses to share, wants his way → spoilt
Reaction to not getting his way → sulked
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'generous' or 'obedient' child would not refuse to share. A child who does not get his way does not usually 'laugh' or 'smile' for hours.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The ______ of the old fort, once the pride of the kingdom, are now ______ with creepers and wild grass.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'once the pride of the kingdom' and 'now' signal decay
solution.explanation: What remains of a fort that was 'once' the pride of a kingdom is its 'ruins', and neglected ruins become 'overgrown with creepers and wild grass'.
steps: What remains of a fort → ruins
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Plans' cannot be overgrown with grass, and 'owners' cannot be covered with creepers. Creepers and wild grass are a sign of neglect, not 'decoration'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
After the accident on the bridge, traffic in both directions ______ for nearly three hours.

solution.concept: Phrase filler: come to a standstill = stop moving completely
solution.explanation: An accident on a bridge blocks the road, so the traffic stops completely for hours: it 'came to a standstill'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Came of age' means became adult or mature, 'came to terms' means accepted something painful, and 'came into its own' means began to show its value; none describes traffic stopping.
solution.final_answer: Option B: came to a standstill

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
Every month, she ______ a small part of her salary for her daughter's education.

solution.concept: Phrase filler: set aside = save or keep for a particular purpose
solution.explanation: Keeping part of one's salary for a particular purpose, here a daughter's education, is 'setting it aside'.
steps: Keeping money for a purpose → set aside
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sets off' means starts a journey or causes, 'sets out' means begins a journey or explains, and 'sets about' means begins a task; none means saving money.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Even as a child, she showed a remarkable ______ for languages, picking up Tamil, Bengali and Marathi from her neighbours.

solution.concept: Single blank: the participle phrase ('picking up three languages') shows natural talent
solution.explanation: A child who picks up three languages from her neighbours has a natural talent for them. 'Flair' means a natural ability: 'a remarkable flair for languages'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Aversion', 'contempt' and 'indifference' all suggest dislike or lack of interest, which contradicts her easy learning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The professor's lectures were so ______ that only a handful of students could follow his arguments.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'so ... that only a handful could follow' points to difficulty
solution.explanation: Lectures that almost nobody can follow are hard to understand. 'Abstruse' means difficult to understand, obscure.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lucid' (clear) and 'succinct' (brief and clear) would make the lectures easy to follow. 'Trite' (overused, unoriginal) ideas are easy to follow too.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The ______ critic found fault with every scene, yet even he ______ that the lead actor was superb.

solution.concept: Double blank: the first word fits 'found fault with every scene'; 'yet even he' signals a reluctant admission
solution.explanation: A critic who finds fault with everything is 'captious'. 'Yet even he' shows that, against his habit, he admitted something good: he 'conceded' that the actor was superb.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Denied' cancels the contrast set up by 'yet even he'. 'Lenient' and 'indulgent' critics do not find fault with every scene, and 'doubted' does not fit 'yet even he'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The young batsman's century in his first match proved to be ______; he did not score another fifty all season.

solution.concept: Phrase filler: a flash in the pan = a sudden success that is not repeated
solution.explanation: One century followed by no other fifty all season is a single success that was never repeated: 'a flash in the pan'.
steps: Clue after the semicolon: no repeat all season
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A red herring' distracts from the real issue, 'a dark horse' is a little-known competitor who surprises everyone (a person, not a century), and 'the order of the day' is something common.
solution.final_answer: Option C: a flash in the pan

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Rather than face the questions directly, the spokesperson gave ______ answers that committed the ministry to nothing.

solution.concept: Single blank: avoiding direct answers and committing to nothing = deliberately vague
solution.explanation: Answers that dodge the questions and commit to nothing are open to more than one reading, deliberately: 'equivocal'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unequivocal', 'categorical' and 'emphatic' answers are clear and firm, the opposite of answers that commit to nothing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'accept' used correctly?

options.text: All the shops are open accept the chemist's.
He works every day accept Sunday.
Everyone accept Ravi came to the party.
Please accept my apologies for the delay.

solution.concept: Accept (verb: to receive or agree to) vs except (preposition: leaving out)
solution.explanation: 'Accept' is a verb meaning to receive willingly. 'Please accept my apologies' uses it correctly.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three need 'except' (leaving out): everyone except Ravi, open except the chemist's, every day except Sunday.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Please accept my apologies for the delay.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) teacher** asked the **(B) blackboard** to clean the **(C) monitor** before the **(D) class** began.

solution.concept: Word swap: who can be asked, and what can be cleaned
solution.explanation: A blackboard cannot be asked to do anything, and a class monitor is not what gets cleaned. Swapping B and C gives 'The teacher asked the monitor to clean the blackboard before the class began.'
steps: 'clean the monitor' should be 'clean the blackboard'
solution.why_others_wrong: A-C gives 'The monitor asked the blackboard to clean the teacher', and A-D gives 'The class asked the blackboard ...'; both remain absurd. The sentence as given makes no sense, so a swap is required.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'ingenious' used correctly?

options.text: Using an old bicycle wheel, the farmer built an ingenious device for lifting water.
She was so ingenious that she believed every stranger's story.
The boy's ingenious answer showed that he was simply honest and innocent.
It would be ingenious of us to pretend that the scheme has no flaws.

solution.concept: Ingenious (clever and inventive) vs ingenuous (innocent, trusting) vs disingenuous (insincere)
solution.explanation: 'Ingenious' means clever and inventive. A water-lifting device made from an old bicycle wheel is an inventive solution, so 'ingenious' fits.
steps: Clever device from a bicycle wheel → ingenious: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The honest-and-innocent answer and the trusting woman need 'ingenuous'; pretending the scheme has no flaws would be 'disingenuous'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Using an old bicycle wheel, the farmer built an ingenious device for lifting water.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'officious' used correctly?

options.text: The results will be declared on the board's officious website next week.
The officious letter from the ministry carried the government's seal.
An officious clerk insisted on checking every visitor's bag, though no one had asked him to.
He remained officious and silent throughout the meeting, giving no opinion.

solution.concept: Officious (too eager to give orders or interfere) vs official (authorised; of an office)
solution.explanation: 'Officious' describes someone who interferes or asserts authority without being asked. A clerk who checks every bag when nobody asked him to is officious.
steps: Letter with a government seal → official
Interfering without being asked → officious: correct
Silent, giving no opinion → not officious (the opposite)
solution.why_others_wrong: The letter and the website need 'official'. A man who stays silent and offers nothing is the opposite of officious.
solution.final_answer: Option C: An officious clerk insisted on checking every visitor's bag, though no one had asked him to.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'scarce' as used in the sentence:
'During the long drought, drinking water became so scarce that tankers were sent to the village every day.'

solution.concept: Scarce = not enough to meet the need
solution.explanation: A drought dries up wells, and tankers had to bring water every day, so there was not enough of it: water was 'in short supply'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Dirty or costly water would not by itself need daily tankers in a drought, and 'plentiful' is the opposite.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'vacant' as used in the sentence:
'Three teachers' posts in the village school have been vacant since March, so the other teachers take extra classes.'

solution.concept: Vacant (of a job or seat) = not filled
solution.explanation: The other teachers take extra classes because no one holds those three posts: they are 'unfilled'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Temporary, well-paid or newly created posts could still be filled; only 'unfilled' explains the extra classes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'hoard' as used in the sentence:
'Fearing a shortage, some traders began to hoard sugar instead of selling it.'

solution.concept: Hoard = collect and keep a large store of something, often secretly
solution.explanation: 'Instead of selling it' shows that the traders kept the sugar back. Storing goods in expectation of a shortage is hoarding: 'store up and hold back'.
steps: They kept it back, fearing a shortage
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sell cheaply' contradicts 'instead of selling it'. Traders fearing a shortage would not throw sugar away, and 'weigh carefully' does not oppose selling.
solution.final_answer: Option B: store up and hold back

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are OPPOSITE in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify antonyms and synonyms
solution.explanation: 'Ascend' means go up and 'descend' means go down, so they are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are synonyms, not opposites.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'cryptic' as used in the sentence:
'The minister's cryptic reply, "Wait and see what the river brings", left the reporters guessing about his plans.'

options.text: having a hidden or puzzling meaning

solution.concept: Cryptic = with a meaning that is hidden or hard to work out
solution.explanation: The reply left reporters 'guessing about his plans', so its meaning was not plain. A remark with a hidden or puzzling meaning is 'cryptic'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing suggests anger, and a one-line reply is not 'long and detailed'. 'Clear and direct' is the opposite; a clear reply would not leave reporters guessing.
solution.final_answer: Option B: having a hidden or puzzling meaning

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'mundane' as used in the sentence:
'After years of adventure at sea, the retired captain found the mundane routine of village life hard to bear.'

solution.concept: Mundane = ordinary, lacking interest or excitement
solution.explanation: The captain is contrasting village life with 'years of adventure'. A routine he finds 'hard to bear' after adventure is ordinary and dull.
steps: Contrast: adventure at sea vs village routine
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Strange and exciting' and 'dangerous' would suit the life at sea, not the village routine. 'Holy' is not suggested by the context.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Arduous' and 'laborious' both mean needing great effort. The other pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
After walking all day in the hot sun, the **weary** travellers sat down under a tree.

solution.concept: Weary = very tired
solution.explanation: People who have walked all day in the hot sun and sit down to rest are worn out: 'weary' means 'tired'.
steps: Context: walked all day in the sun, then sat down
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing suggests the travellers were 'cheerful', 'careless' or 'foreign'; the context is about exhaustion.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **dexterous** potter shaped a perfect jar on the wheel in under a minute.

solution.concept: Dexterous = skilful, especially with the hands
solution.explanation: Shaping a perfect jar in under a minute shows great skill with the hands: the potter is 'skilful'.
steps: Context: perfect jar in under a minute
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Clumsy' is the opposite. Nothing about age is said, and a potter who works in under a minute is fast rather than 'patient'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **ominous** silence in the forest made the villagers fear that a tiger was nearby.

solution.concept: Ominous = suggesting that something bad is going to happen
solution.explanation: The silence made the villagers fear a tiger, so it seemed to warn of danger. That is 'threatening'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A silence that causes fear is not 'pleasant', and a silence cannot be 'noisy'. 'Ancient' has nothing to do with fear.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Many offices have stopped using fax machines, which are now largely **obsolete**.

solution.concept: Obsolete = out of date; no longer used
solution.explanation: Offices 'have stopped using' fax machines because newer methods have replaced them, so the machines are out of date: 'outmoded'.
steps: Clue: offices have stopped using them
Replaced by newer methods = out of date
solution.why_others_wrong: Cost and fragility are not mentioned as reasons, and 'novel' (new) contradicts offices giving them up.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **surreptitious** glances that the clerk kept casting at the open safe made the guard suspicious.

solution.concept: Surreptitious = done secretly, so as not to be noticed
solution.explanation: The glances made the guard suspicious because they were secret and sly. 'Furtive' means secretive and sly, trying to avoid notice.
steps: Glances meant not to be noticed
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Candid' (open) is the opposite. 'Admiring' and 'indifferent' do not explain why the guard grew suspicious.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Though eighty, my grandfather is still **robust** and walks five kilometres every morning.

solution.concept: Robust = strong and healthy; opposite: frail (weak and delicate)
solution.explanation: A man of eighty who walks five kilometres every day is strong and healthy, i.e. 'robust'. The opposite is 'frail'.
steps: Context: walks 5 km daily at eighty
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Healthy' is close to a synonym. 'Cheerful' and 'tall' are not related to strength.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Relations between the two firms were **cordial** for years, until a dispute over a contract soured them.

solution.concept: Cordial = warm and friendly; opposite: hostile (unfriendly, antagonistic)
solution.explanation: The relations were warm and friendly until a dispute 'soured them'. The opposite of 'cordial' is 'hostile'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Friendly' and 'courteous' are close to synonyms. 'Lengthy' describes duration, not the warmth of relations.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Even when the crowd began shouting, the **phlegmatic** umpire calmly checked the replay before giving his decision.

solution.concept: Phlegmatic = calm and not easily excited; opposite: excitable
solution.explanation: The umpire stayed calm while the crowd shouted, which is what 'phlegmatic' means. The opposite is 'excitable'.
steps: Context: calm despite a shouting crowd
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unhurried' is close to the meaning, not opposite. 'Impartial' and 'experienced' describe other qualities of an umpire.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to cry over spilt milk'.

options.text: to complain about small household expenses
to regret something that has already happened and cannot be changed
to weep at a sad story

solution.concept: Idiom: cry over spilt milk = be upset about something that cannot be undone
solution.explanation: Milk that has been spilt cannot be put back. To 'cry over spilt milk' is to waste time regretting something that cannot be changed.
steps: Spilt milk = something done that cannot be undone
solution.why_others_wrong: The idiom is not about wasting food, household expenses or sad stories; these read it literally.
solution.final_answer: Option B: to regret something that has already happened and cannot be changed

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom in bold.
The landlord had already raised the rent twice that year, so his demand for an extra month's deposit was **the last straw**, and the tenants moved out.

options.text: the first sign of a coming quarrel
a generous offer that was refused
the final problem in a series that makes a situation unbearable

solution.concept: Idiom: the last straw = the last of a series of troubles, after which one cannot bear any more
solution.explanation: After two rent increases, one more demand was too much, and the tenants left. That final demand was 'the last straw'.
solution.why_others_wrong: The demand came after earlier troubles, so it was not the 'first sign'. It drove the tenants away, so it was neither 'harmless' nor 'generous'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: the final problem in a series that makes a situation unbearable

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'Hobson's choice'.

options.text: a choice between two equally good options
a situation in which there is only one option, so no real choice
a choice that is made for someone by a friend
a choice made after careful thought

solution.concept: Idiom: Hobson's choice = take what is offered or nothing
solution.explanation: The phrase comes from a stable-keeper who let customers take only the horse nearest the door, or none at all. A 'Hobson's choice' is therefore no real choice.
steps: Origin: take this one or none
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Careful thought', 'two equally good options' and a choice made by a friend all assume a real choice exists, which is exactly what the idiom denies.
solution.final_answer: Option B: a situation in which there is only one option, so no real choice

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom in bold.
After months of publicity, the much-awaited film festival turned out to be **a damp squib**: half the films never arrived and the halls were empty.

solution.concept: Idiom: a damp squib = something expected to be impressive that turns out to be a disappointment
solution.explanation: A squib is a small firework; a damp one fails to go off. After 'months of publicity', a festival with missing films and empty halls was a disappointing failure.
solution.why_others_wrong: Empty halls rule out 'a surprising success'. A festival is not described as 'quiet', and cost is never mentioned.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom in bold.
Asked whether he supported the new tax, the MLA chose to **sit on the fence**, saying that both sides had valid points.

solution.concept: Idiom: sit on the fence = avoid committing oneself to either side
solution.explanation: By saying that 'both sides had valid points', the MLA avoided supporting or opposing the tax: he sat on the fence.
solution.why_others_wrong: Strong opposition is a clear position, the opposite of the idiom. Nothing suggests a sudden change of mind or a break.
solution.final_answer: Option A: avoid taking either side

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to carry coals to Newcastle'.

options.text: to bring bad news to someone who is far away
to supply something to a place or person that already has plenty of it
to do hard physical work for very little pay
to travel a long distance for an important purpose

solution.concept: Idiom: carry coals to Newcastle = do something pointless because what is brought is already plentiful there
solution.explanation: Newcastle in England was a great coal-mining town. Carrying coal there was pointless. The idiom means supplying something to a place that already has plenty of it.
steps: Meaning: supplying what is already plentiful
solution.why_others_wrong: The idiom has nothing to do with low pay, long journeys or bad news; these read 'carrying coal' literally.
solution.final_answer: Option B: to supply something to a place or person that already has plenty of it

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A large building in which aircraft are kept and repaired

solution.concept: One-word substitution: hangar (aircraft shed); do not confuse with hanger (for clothes)
solution.explanation: A 'hangar' is a large building where aircraft are housed and serviced.
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'hanger' holds clothes, a 'harbour' shelters ships, and a 'garage' is for cars.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person who walks while asleep

solution.concept: One-word substitution: somn- (sleep) + ambul- (walk)
solution.explanation: 'Somnambulist' (from Latin somnus, sleep, and ambulare, to walk) means a sleepwalker.
solution.why_others_wrong: An 'insomniac' cannot sleep, a 'ventriloquist' makes his voice seem to come from elsewhere, and a 'hypochondriac' constantly fears being ill.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person who dislikes and distrusts other people and avoids their company

solution.concept: One-word substitution: mis- (hatred) + anthrop- (humankind)
solution.explanation: A 'misanthrope' dislikes humankind in general and avoids other people.
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'philanthropist' loves people and helps them, a 'misogynist' dislikes women in particular, and an 'ascetic' gives up comforts for spiritual reasons, not out of dislike of people.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
We can solve this problem easily.

options.text: This problem could be solve easily.
This problem can be solving easily.
This problem can be solved easily.

solution.concept: Passive with a modal: modal + be + past participle
solution.explanation: The object 'this problem' becomes the subject; 'can solve' becomes 'can be solved'. 'By us' may be left out because it adds nothing.
steps: can + be + past participle → can be solved
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Can solved' leaves out 'be'; 'could be solve' changes the modal and uses the base form; 'can be solving' uses the -ing form instead of the past participle.
solution.final_answer: Option D: This problem can be solved easily.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
It is time to close the shop.

options.text: It is time for the shop to close.
The shop is time to be closed.
It is time to be closed the shop.
It is time for the shop to be closed.

solution.concept: Passive of 'It is time + to-infinitive': It is time for + object + to be + past participle
solution.explanation: The object of 'to close' is 'the shop'. In the passive, the infinitive becomes 'to be closed' and the shop is brought in with 'for': 'It is time for the shop to be closed.'
steps: Infinitive with object: to close the shop
'It is time for the shop to be closed.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'For the shop to close' keeps an active infinitive (the shop closes itself). 'To be closed the shop' leaves the object after a passive verb. 'The shop is time ...' makes no sense.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It is time for the shop to be closed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
He said to me, "Thank you for your help."

options.text: He thanked me for my help.
He thanked to me for his help.
He told me that thank you for his help.
He said me thank you for my help.

solution.concept: Reporting thanks: 'said ... "Thank you"' becomes 'thanked'; pronouns change to suit the speaker and listener
solution.explanation: Words of thanks are reported with the verb 'thank'. 'Your help' (the listener's help) becomes 'my help' when the listener ('me') reports it: 'He thanked me for my help.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Said me' is wrong ('say' does not take a person as object). 'Thanked to me' adds a wrong 'to', and 'his help' changes whose help it was. 'Told me that thank you' keeps the direct words inside a that-clause.
solution.final_answer: Option A: He thanked me for my help.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
She said to him, "You look tired. Why don't you rest for a while?"

options.text: She told him that he looks tired and asked why don't you rest for a while.
She told him that he looked tired and suggested that he should rest for a while.
She told him that he looked tired and suggested him to rest for a while.
She said him that he looked tired and suggested that he should rest for a while.

solution.concept: Mixed narration: a statement (told ... that) + a suggestion ('Why don't you ...?' → suggested that ... should)
solution.explanation: 'You look tired' is a statement: 'told him that he looked tired' (tense backshifted). 'Why don't you rest?' is a suggestion, not a real question, so it is reported with 'suggested that he should rest'.
steps: Statement → told him that he looked tired
'Why don't you ...?' = suggestion → suggested that he should ...
solution.why_others_wrong: Keeping 'looks' and 'why don't you' copies the direct words. 'Suggested him to rest' is wrong: 'suggest' takes a that-clause or -ing, not object + infinitive. 'Said him' is wrong ('say' needs 'to').
solution.final_answer: Option B: She told him that he looked tired and suggested that he should rest for a while.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
The goods ______ loaded onto the lorry late last night.

solution.concept: 'Goods' (merchandise) is always plural and takes a plural verb
solution.explanation: 'Goods' has no singular form in this sense and is treated as plural; the time is past ('last night'): 'The goods were loaded ...'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Was' and 'is' are singular, and 'is' is also present. 'Has loaded' would make the goods do the loading.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
The United States ______ a federal system of government.

solution.concept: A country's name that is plural in form takes a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'The United States' names one country, so it takes a singular verb: 'The United States has a federal system of government.'
steps: Subject: one country, plural in form
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Have', 'are having' and 'were having' treat the country as plural; the last two also use 'have' (possess) in a continuous form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
All the riches of the old merchant ______ not able to buy him a single night of peaceful sleep.

solution.concept: 'Riches' (wealth) is a plural noun and takes a plural verb
solution.explanation: 'Riches' has no singular in this sense and is always plural, so the verb is plural; the story is in the past: 'All the riches ... were not able to buy him ...'.
steps: 'of the old merchant' does not change the number
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Was' and 'is' treat 'riches' as singular. 'Has not able' is not a correct verb form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
So far this season, our school team ______ four matches and lost none.

solution.concept: Present perfect with 'so far': a period that runs up to now
solution.explanation: 'So far this season' covers the time from the start of the season up to now, which calls for the present perfect: 'has won four matches and (has) lost none'.
steps: Time marker: so far (up to now)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Had won' needs a later past moment to refer to. 'Wins' and 'is winning' cannot count matches already played up to now.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
The window is still open and the jewellery box is empty; the thief seems ______ through the window.

solution.concept: Perfect infinitive (to have + past participle) for an action earlier than the main verb
solution.explanation: The seeming is present ('seems'), but the escape happened earlier. An earlier action after 'seem' takes the perfect infinitive: 'the thief seems to have escaped through the window.'
steps: Earlier action → perfect infinitive: 'to have escaped'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'To escape' would describe a present or habitual action. 'Seems escaping' is not standard, and 'to be escaped' is a wrong passive.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Yesterday morning, she assured her manager that by six o'clock that evening she ______ the report.

solution.concept: Sequence of tenses: future perfect seen from the past = would have + past participle
solution.explanation: Her promise was made in the past ('assured', 'yesterday morning') about a time that is also past now (six o'clock that evening). 'Will have finished' moves back to 'would have finished'.
steps: Future perfect from a past viewpoint
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Will have finished' ignores the past reporting verb, and six o'clock yesterday is no longer in the future. 'Has finished' and 'had been finishing' do not express a promise about a deadline.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Meena is ______ only daughter of her parents.

solution.concept: 'The' before 'only' when it picks out a single, particular person or thing
solution.explanation: 'Only daughter' names the one and only daughter, so the definite article is needed: 'Meena is the only daughter of her parents.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A' and 'an' would suggest one of several, which contradicts 'only'. Without an article the noun phrase is incomplete.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in ______ Bay of Bengal.

solution.concept: 'The' with groups of islands and with bays named 'the Bay of ...'
solution.explanation: A group of islands takes 'the' (the Andaman and Nicobar Islands), and so does a bay named with 'of' (the Bay of Bengal).
solution.why_others_wrong: Dropping either 'the' breaks one of the two rules. 'An' is singular and cannot go with 'Islands'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The old soldier is blind ______ one eye but still reads the newspaper every morning.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: blind in (one eye)
solution.explanation: Loss of sight in one eye is expressed as 'blind in one eye'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Blind at', 'blind from' and 'blind by' one eye are not used; 'blind to' means unwilling to notice something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
By selling two of their goats, the family managed to ______ hunger until the next harvest.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: stave off = keep something bad away for a time
solution.explanation: Selling the goats gave the family money for food, which kept hunger away until the harvest. To keep a danger at bay for a while is to 'stave it off'.
steps: Result: hunger kept away for a time
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Make off' means run away, 'set off' means start a journey or cause (an alarm), and 'lay off' means dismiss workers; none means keeping hunger away.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ the bell rang, the children ran out of the classroom.

solution.concept: 'As soon as' = immediately after
solution.explanation: The children ran out immediately after the bell rang: 'As soon as the bell rang, the children ran out of the classroom.'
steps: Event 2 follows at once: the children ran out
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unless' sets a condition that does not fit a past event, 'Although' signals a contrast that is not there, and 'So that' would make the bell ring for the purpose of the children running out.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
The scholarship is open only to first-time students; ______, anyone who has already earned a degree cannot apply.

solution.concept: 'In other words' introduces a restatement of the same point
solution.explanation: 'Open only to first-time students' and 'anyone who already has a degree cannot apply' say the same thing in two ways. A restatement is introduced by 'in other words'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'On the other hand' and 'by contrast' signal a contrast, and 'even so' signals a surprising contrast; the second clause does not contrast with the first.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
The new rules will add to the paperwork of small lenders. ______, they will give depositors far better protection.

solution.concept: 'Be that as it may' = even though that is true (accepting a point, then moving to a stronger one)
solution.explanation: The opening sentence admits a drawback (more paperwork); the next gives an outweighing benefit. 'Be that as it may' accepts the first point and turns to the second.
steps: Sentence 2: a benefit that outweighs it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Inasmuch as' (= because), 'Lest' (= for fear that) and 'So long as' (= provided that) introduce clauses, and none of them can open a full sentence that answers a drawback.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Be that as it may
